title: FAA Lifts Nationwide Ground Stop After Hours-Long Telecom Outage; Weekend Disruptions Continue
dek: The FAA lifted a four-hour nationwide ground stop Friday evening. On Saturday, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the system was back at full operations, but delays and cancellations persisted.
author: Meridian Newsroom

image.alt: The FAA air traffic control tower at Philadelphia International Airport

keyPoints: The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon and lifted it at 8:15 p.m. ET; USA TODAY places the start at 3:36 p.m. ET, while other outlets gave slightly later times.
Duffy blamed aging equipment on Friday; on Saturday he said the trouble began when a contractor replacing copper wire with fiber at one remote site installed a router that flooded others.
Officials were still determining whether the cause was an installation error or a faulty router, Duffy said, per USA TODAY.
USA TODAY, citing FlightAware, reported more than 5,100 flights delayed or canceled on Nov. 14; the paper said it was not clear how many were caused by the ground stop.
Duffy said the FAA is “back at full operations” but warned that carriers would keep rescheduling flights for some time.
body:
The Federal Aviation Administration halted departures across the United States on Friday afternoon, citing “extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety,” after a telecommunications outage affected multiple air route traffic control centers. The agency lifted the ground stop Friday evening after more than four hours, according to CNBC and Al Jazeera.

## Timing and cause

Accounts differ slightly on when the stop began. Al Jazeera reported that the FAA issued it at 3:54 p.m. ET. USA TODAY quoted Duffy saying that instability in radar and communications systems began at 3:36 p.m. ET. CNBC said the stop was issued at about 4 p.m. ET and canceled at 8:15 p.m. ET; USA TODAY said the cancellation came around 8:30 p.m. ET.

Duffy told reporters that the system’s aging technology was to blame. He said analog switches and routers had become overloaded and produced inconsistent data, which led the FAA to shut the system down. CNBC quoted Duffy saying the routers “went down.” Mullin said there was no indication of a threat and that the outage “appears this was mechanically driven,” according to CNBC. CNN reported that Mullin said the stop was not linked to a Microsoft outage earlier that week.

## Scale of the disruption

CNBC reported that more than 10,000 flights were disrupted during the stop. CNN reported that more than 15,000 U.S. flights were delayed or canceled on Friday and that about 3,000 were expected to be delayed or canceled on Saturday. Aviation analytics firm Cirium told Al Jazeera that at least 827 flights had been diverted by 7:05 p.m. ET, and that 670 of them returned to their departure airports.

USA TODAY reported that American Airlines and United warned of residual delays and cancellations, and that Delta let customers change flights at no extra cost. CNBC, citing a memo, reported that JetBlue planned to cancel the rest of Friday’s flights, apart from European routes, along with Saturday flights, so crews and planes could be in place.

## What officials said about recovery

Duffy said flights would not resume immediately and that the recovery would be “going to be slow,” depending on the availability of pilots and flight attendants, according to Al Jazeera and CNN. He urged Congress to fund improvements to the system, and said the disruption should not affect Thanksgiving travel a couple of weeks away, CNN reported.

Al Jazeera and CNBC both described the stop as only the second nationwide ground stop of departures since the September 11, 2001 attacks. CNBC said the previous one was in January 2023, after a failure of a pilot communication system.

## Saturday: flights still disrupted

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Saturday that the problem began when a contractor at one of the FAA’s remote locations was replacing aging copper wire with fiber, work he said has been going on for decades. He said the router installed at that site began flooding others on the air traffic control system, causing communication problems and disruption to radar feeds. Officials were still working to determine whether the cause was an installation error or a faulty router, Duffy said, [USA TODAY reported](https://usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2026/11/14/flight-airports-delays-cancellations-faa-ground-stop/92778770007). He also said, “We are back at full operations.”

The contractor installation detail does not appear in the Friday reporting reviewed for this story, when Duffy blamed overloaded analog switches and routers. The root cause has not been established.

Delays and cancellations continued. USA TODAY cited FlightAware data showing more than 5,100 flights into or out of the United States delayed or canceled on Nov. 14, while noting that it was not clear how many resulted from the ground stop. The paper reported that Atlanta, Chicago O’Hare, New York’s JFK and Dallas-Fort Worth were among the hardest-hit hubs. Duffy said, “You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft and crews where they are needed most.” He had earlier said it would take “some time” to return to full capacity, without giving a timeline.

## What is not yet known

The reporting reviewed for this story does not include a detailed technical root-cause report from the FAA. Duffy urged passengers to check with their airlines for the status of their flights.
